author: high
claim: Let n be a positive integer and let x_1,...,x_{n^2+1} be distinct real numbers. The sequence contains a strictly increasing subsequence of length n+1 or a strictly decreasing subsequence of length n+1.
evidence: For every index i, let P_i be the maximum length of a strictly increasing subsequence ending at x_i, and let D_i be the maximum length of a strictly decreasing subsequence ending at x_i. Suppose neither required subsequence exists. Then 1<=P_i<=n and 1<=D_i<=n for every i. If i<j, distinctness gives exactly one of x_i<x_j and x_i>x_j. In the first case, append x_j to a longest increasing subsequence ending at x_i; hence P_j>=P_i+1. In the second case, append x_j to a longest decreasing subsequence ending at x_i; hence D_j>=D_i+1. Therefore (P_i,D_i)!=(P_j,D_j) whenever i<j. Thus the n^2+1 indices yield n^2+1 distinct pairs in {1,...,n}x{1,...,n}, which has only n^2 elements, a contradiction.

glossary.x_i: the real number at position i in the given sequence
glossary.P_i: maximum length of a strictly increasing subsequence ending at position i
glossary.D_i: maximum length of a strictly decreasing subsequence ending at position i
